summary: A 1970 note proposing a user-oriented protocol to connect to services by name instead of by number. It is a proposal in the early series.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 76 proposes letting network users request a connection by a symbolic name, such as a device name or file label. The destination host looks up the corresponding socket and reports whether the item exists and is available.

questions: connection by name user oriented protocol
how did rfc 76 look up a socket number
what commands were in the terminal user control language
subtitle: A proposal to request network connections by symbolic names instead of socket numbers.

tldr.problem: Users of a network-only site found it difficult to manage connections by numeric socket values and other protocol details.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal lets a user identify a device, process or file by a label, then asks the destination host for the socket number associated with that label.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives protocol extensions and an example user session, but does not state that the proposal was adopted.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 76 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC describes a proposed connection-by-name protocol and an example user interface.

sections.title: Why Connect by Name
sections.content:
The Center for Advanced Computation at the University of Illinois expected to use the ARPA Network as a port to computing resources at other nodes. Its prospective users were confused by having to handle socket numbers and links directly.

The authors propose a user-level interface that uses symbolic names and lets system procedures translate them into host-to-host protocol operations. The destination host knows its socket-number space and the status of the user or process attached to each socket.
sections.plainLanguage: Users at the Center needed connections to resources at other network sites, but socket numbers exposed protocol details. The proposal lets users name the resource and leaves the lookup to the hosts.

sections.title: Labels and Socket Lookup
sections.content:
A label can be a device name or a user code and filename. The suggested device names include LP for line printer, CR for card reader, DSK for disk and TTY for a teletype-compatible terminal. The RFC notes that some systems use multi-part file identifiers.

The proposed RFSNL request asks the destination host for the socket number attached to a label. The destination can report that the resource exists, that it exists but is unavailable, or that no such resource exists.
sections.plainLanguage: A user asks for a named device or file instead of supplying its socket number. The destination host replies with the socket information and whether the resource is available.

sections.title: Example User Session
sections.content:
The example follows a user at the University of Illinois Center for Advanced Computation controlling processes at Utah and at the ILLIAC site. The user issues commands using host and file names while the host software requests and exchanges socket numbers behind the scenes.

The example also shows requests being queued while the system retries a connection and data being copied between network resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The example user names remote systems and files in commands. The local and destination hosts handle the socket lookup and connection setup.

sections.title: The Terminal User Control Language
sections.content:
The appendix gives a preliminary control language for a proposed PDP-11 network terminal system. It includes commands to link to a host, copy data, end a connection, identify a user, check device status, send a message and assign or label devices.

The note explains that a flag character distinguishes commands for the local system from input sent to a connected process. It describes the language as an initial attempt and leaves some topics for later documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix lists commands for connecting to hosts, copying data and managing devices. A special flag marks commands meant for the local system rather than the remote process.
